title: Immutability Helper

sections.Thought Process (as if you’re the interv:
- Start with a brute-force:  
  Deep clone the entire object, apply the mutator to the clone, and return it.  
  - **Problem:** Wasteful for large objects (up to 4·10^5 characters, with many `produce` calls) when only a tiny change is made.
- Optimize with **copy-on-write** using a **Proxy**:
  - Each container (object/array) the mutator touches is tracked by a small node: its original, a lazily created shallow copy, and a link to its parent.
  - `get`: read from the copy if one exists, otherwise from the original. If the value is itself an object/array, return a (cached) child proxy so nested access works.
  - `set`: on the first real write, shallow-copy the container, and also copy every ancestor up to the root, pointing each ancestor's copy at the new child copy.
  - Untouched branches are kept by reference (structural sharing), and the original is never written to.
- Tradeoff:  
  - Slightly more code and bookkeeping, but only the root-to-change paths are copied instead of the whole tree.
sections.Corner cases to consider:
- Reading a value after writing it in the same mutator (must come from the copy, e.g. `proxy.arr[0]` after `proxy.arr[0] = 5`).
- Setting a key to the value it already has (no need to copy anything).
- A mutator that makes no change (still return an object that is safe to use; the original must not be modified).
- Adding a brand-new key to an existing container (allowed; it just goes on the copy).
- Arrays as the input or nested (index writes and `length` reads work through the same traps).
- Several `produce` calls on the same helper must each start from the original, not from earlier results.
sections.Time and Space complexity Analysis:
- **Time Complexity:**  
  - Each read or write through the proxy is O(1), except the first write into a container, which shallow-copies it (O(its width)) and every not-yet-copied ancestor on the path to the root.
  - Worst case: O(N), where N is the total size of the object/array (if every container is changed).
  - Typical case: O(sum of the widths of the containers on the changed root-to-leaf paths).

- **Space Complexity:**  
  - O(total width of the containers that were copied), at most O(N); untouched branches are shared, not copied.
  - Plus O(number of touched containers) for the nodes and child proxies.
sections.Potential follow-up questions (as if you:
- Can you avoid copying the root at all when nothing was changed?  
  *Hint: Return `root.copy ?? this.obj`, at the risk of handing back the same reference.*

- What if the mutator may delete keys or call `push`/`splice`?  
  *Hint: Add a `deleteProperty` trap and route array methods through the proxy, so they hit the `get`/`set` traps on the copy.*

- What if the mutator may assign objects, like `proxy.x = {}`?  
  *Hint: Clear the cached child proxy for that key, since the child's original is no longer what the parent holds.*
sections.Summary:
The solution leverages the **proxy pattern** and lazy (on-write) shallow copying to provide efficient, user-friendly immutable-object "modification".  
This is known as *structural sharing*, and is the idea behind libraries like Immer and the update model of Redux/React state. It is a foundational technique for persistent (functional) data structures and undo history.  
The coding pattern generalizes to any situation where local modifications to large, nested data must be efficient and non-destructive.
sections.Flashcard: Wrap the object in a Proxy with get/set traps: reads come from a lazily made shallow copy or the original (returning child proxies for nested objects), the first write copies the container and its ancestors up to the root, leaving untouched branches shared.
